implementation_notes: Rust's standard library has no multi-consumer queue: std::sync::mpsc and tokio::sync::mpsc are both explicitly multi-producer, single-consumer. The idiomatic competing-consumer pool is therefore crossbeam-channel (bounded or unbounded MPMC) with N std::thread workers that clone the receiver and loop on recv(); each Job is moved into exactly one worker, so there is no shared mutable state and no lock in the hot path. Bounded channels apply backpressure by blocking send, and dropping the sender closes the queue so `while let Ok(job) = rx.recv()` terminates cleanly.
pitfalls: A worker that panics while holding a job loses it silently; without a broker there is no redelivery unless you catch and requeue.
An unbounded channel hides overload as memory growth - capacity is the flow-control knob, and send() blocking is the backpressure.
Cloning the receiver is required: moving the single Receiver into a closure sends only one worker the messages and the others exit immediately.

variants.name: Tokio tasks over an async MPMC channel
variants.idiom_name: Tokio tasks over an async MPMC channel
variants.implementation_notes: In the async ecosystem the competition needs an MPMC-capable channel because tokio::sync::mpsc is single-consumer: spawn N workers over an async-channel or flume receiver (or wrap tokio's Receiver in Arc<Mutex<_>>, which serialises the receive), and let the runtime multiplex the tasks. The pattern then holds across many lightweight tasks instead of OS threads, at the price of an extra dependency and a runtime - and acknowledgement/redelivery remain the application's or broker client's job.
pitfalls: tokio::sync::mpsc cannot be shared between tasks: N workers on one Receiver do not compile (or require a Mutex that serialises receive).
A blocking call inside an async worker stalls the runtime worker thread; use spawn_blocking for sync handlers.
Cancelling a worker task mid-handle abandons the job without acknowledgement - only cancel at safe points or let the broker redeliver.
